drills.q: Walk through the compiler pipeline stage by stage and name each stage's concrete output artifact.
drills.a: Lexer: source text -> token stream. Parser: tokens -> AST. Lowering/semantic analysis: AST -> IR (normalized, often SSA-form, explicit basic-block control-flow graph). Optimization: IR -> optimized IR (same semantics, better properties). Codegen: optimized IR -> machine code via instruction selection and register allocation.

drills.q: Define SSA and explain why it turns most classical optimizations into a local rather than whole-program problem.
drills.a: Static Single Assignment requires every variable to be assigned exactly once textually, with phi nodes reconciling values arriving from different control-flow predecessors at merge points. Because each name has exactly one definition site, 'what value does this hold here' is answered by looking at one place instead of tracing backward through all possible reassignments -- which is what makes constant propagation, DCE, and CSE tractable as local passes.

drills.q: Explain why inlining is considered the most impactful compiler optimization beyond simply removing call/ret overhead.
drills.a: Inlining exposes the callee's instructions directly within the caller's optimization context, unlocking every other pass (constant propagation, dead-code elimination, register allocation) to operate across what used to be an opaque function boundary -- a caller's known argument value can now flow into and simplify the callee's body. The call/ret savings are real but secondary to this cascading unlock effect.

drills.q: A loop that looks obviously vectorizable isn't being vectorized. What's the diagnostic process, and give one genuinely non-vectorizable and one vectorizable-but-order-changing example.
drills.a: Check the compiler's missed-optimization report first (-fopt-info-vec-missed on GCC, -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize on Clang) for the specific blocking reason -- unproven aliasing, a loop-carried dependency, an unanalyzable call -- rather than guessing or reaching for intrinsics. Non-vectorizable: a[i] = a[i-1] * 2 (true loop-carried dependency on the prior result). Vectorizable-but-order-changing: sum += a[i], a reduction usable via multiple partial-sum lanes, but this changes floating-point rounding order since addition isn't associative.

drills.q: Why does restrict matter for vectorization correctness, and what happens if you falsely mark aliasing pointers as restrict?
drills.a: restrict promises the compiler that a pointer doesn't alias certain others in scope; without it, the compiler must conservatively assume aliasing is possible and can't safely reorder memory accesses across loop iterations. If the promise is true, the compiler can prove reordering safe and vectorize. If you lie -- mark genuinely aliasing pointers as restrict -- it's undefined behavior: the compiler generates code assuming no aliasing, and if the arrays actually overlap in a way that matters, results become unspecified and can vary by optimization level or compiler.

drills.q: Explain register allocation's core problem and what a 'spill' is, including how it's visible in disassembly.
drills.a: IR uses an effectively unlimited number of virtual registers/SSA values; the target ISA has a small fixed physical register set (16 GPRs x86-64, 31 ARM64). Register allocation maps virtual to physical registers, and when more values are simultaneously live than available physical registers, some are spilled -- stored to a stack slot and reloaded on demand, trading a register access for a memory access. Visible in disassembly as [rbp-N]-style stack loads/stores in code that would otherwise be register-to-register.

drills.q: Compare what PGO and JIT compilation are both trying to achieve and explain where their tradeoffs diverge.
drills.a: Both use real observed program behavior rather than static heuristics to guide optimization decisions (hot branches, monomorphic call sites, actual loop trip counts). PGO does this ahead-of-time: an instrumented/sampled training run feeds a profile into a subsequent static compile, shipping a statically-optimized binary with zero runtime warmup cost but requiring representative training traffic. A JIT does this continuously at runtime, adapting live to actual behavior but paying warmup cost and able to deoptimize if runtime behavior later diverges from earlier assumptions.

drills.q: Why can a vectorized floating-point reduction produce a numerically different result than the scalar version, and under what compiler conditions is this transformation actually permitted?
drills.a: Floating-point addition is not associative -- rounding at each step depends on operand order -- so summing via multiple SIMD-lane partial accumulators computes a genuinely different order than strict sequential left-to-right accumulation, producing a different (typically very close) rounded result. This is not a bug (both orderings are valid under IEEE-754), but compilers are only permitted to make this transformation under relaxed floating-point flags (e.g. -ffast-math or specific looser contract flags), not under strict default IEEE compliance, precisely because they're aware it changes results.

drills.q: What architectural decision makes LLVM easier to retarget to new hardware backends than a more monolithic compiler design, and what's the practical maintenance gotcha this creates?
drills.a: LLVM is architected around a stable, well-specified SSA-form IR that frontends and backends target independently -- a new backend implements instruction selection and register allocation against that one IR (via TableGen machine descriptions) without touching the frontend or shared optimizer. Gotcha: LLVM IR is not guaranteed stable across LLVM versions the way a wire protocol would be, so projects depending on it as core infrastructure (e.g. Rust) must carefully track compatible LLVM versions -- a real, ongoing maintenance burden.

drills.q: Staff-level: make the cost-benefit case for enabling both LTO and PGO on a latency-sensitive service's release pipeline, and describe how you'd detect a stale PGO profile actively hurting performance.
drills.a: Benefit: LTO lets the optimizer see across translation-unit boundaries (inlining across .c files), and PGO focuses aggressive optimization on genuinely hot paths from real traffic rather than static heuristics -- together commonly cited for single-digit to low-double-digit percent gains on performance-critical services. Cost: LTO can substantially increase link time and peak memory usage on large codebases; PGO requires maintaining and periodically refreshing a training/profiling step. Detecting staleness: compare current production behavior via live profiling/observability against what the PGO-guided binary assumed was hot -- a mismatch (optimized-for call patterns or branches that no longer reflect current traffic) is the concrete signal, fixed by re-running training against current representative traffic rather than abandoning PGO.
